Approach and limitations

Source: vignettes/approach_and_limitations.Rmd
approach_and_limitations.Rmd

This vignette explains the reasoning behind statomatic’s approach, and what to keep in mind when using it. It includes simulations that measure how well statomatic sorts rows, and what happens when a row is sorted into the wrong set.

The approach

Tests like the ANOVA rely on assumptions about the data: the residuals should be normally distributed and the groups should have equal variances. In high-throughput data, thousands of rows (genes, taxa, metabolites, …) are tested at once, and some rows will meet these assumptions while others won’t. Applying one test to every row ignores this.

Statomatic checks the assumptions for each row separately, and chooses a test that suits that row:

Set Meaning 2 groups > 2 groups > 2 groups: pairwise comparisons
ne normal, equal variance t-test ANOVA Tukey HSD
nu normal, unequal variance Welch test Welch test Dunnett T3
nn not normal Wilcoxon test Kruskal-Wallis test Dunn test

A row is sorted into nn if the Shapiro-Wilk test on its residuals has p < 0.05 (shapiro_threshold). Otherwise, it is sorted into nu if Levene’s test has p < 0.05 (levene_threshold), and into ne if not.

The tests element of the results shows the Shapiro-Wilk and Levene p-values of every row and the set it was sorted into, so you can see how each row was handled.

How well does the sorting work?

The Shapiro-Wilk and Levene tests are themselves statistical tests. How often they detect non-normality or unequal variances depends on the number of samples: with few samples per group, they often miss them.

To measure this, we simulated rows for which the right set is known, and sorted them with test_norm(). Each scenario has three groups of the same size and 500 simulated rows:

  • normal, equal variance: normally distributed, all groups with SD 1 (should be sorted into ne)
  • normal, unequal variance: normally distributed, one group with an SD 3 or 5 times larger (should be sorted into nu)
  • skewed: log-normally distributed (should be sorted into nn)

The table shows the percentage of rows sorted into the right set:

Percentage of rows sorted into the right set
Scenario 4 per group 5 per group 6 per group 8 per group 12 per group 20 per group
normal, equal variance 90 94 92 90 88 92
normal, unequal variance (SD 3:1) 23 11 31 40 38 22
normal, unequal variance (SD 5:1) 29 20 29 25 7 1
skewed 31 42 57 78 96 100

Scenario Samples per group % sorted into ne % sorted into nu % sorted into nn

normal, unequal variance (SD 3:1) 6 42 31 27
normal, unequal variance (SD 3:1) 8 26 40 35
normal, unequal variance (SD 3:1) 12 7 38 55

normal, unequal variance (SD 5:1) 4 32 29 39
normal, unequal variance (SD 5:1) 5 37 20 43
normal, unequal variance (SD 5:1) 6 15 29 55

skewed 6 36 7 57

Two things stand out:

  1. With few samples, most rows are sorted into ne. Normal rows with equal variance are sorted correctly about 90% of the time at every group size, which is expected: with a threshold of 0.05, each of the two checks wrongly flags about 5% of these rows. But with 4 to 6 samples per group, which is common, many skewed rows and many rows with unequal variances are also sorted into ne, because the checks don’t have enough samples to detect the problem.

  2. Rows with unequal variances are often sorted into nn. The Shapiro-Wilk test is applied to the residuals of all groups together. When one group is much more spread out than the others, these pooled residuals have heavier tails than a normal distribution, so the row is sorted into nn before Levene’s test is reached, even though each group is normally distributed. This happens more often with more samples, because the Shapiro-Wilk test then detects the heavier tails more easily.

What happens when a row is sorted into the wrong set?

A row in the wrong set is analyzed with a test that doesn’t suit it. To see what this means, we simulated rows with equal group means, so that every p-value below 0.05 is a false positive, and tested them with run_anova(), run_welch() and run_kruskal(). The third group has an SD of 1, 3 or 5 times that of the other groups. Each scenario has 5,000 simulated rows. The false-positive rate should be 5%:

False-positive rate at p < 0.05, with equal group means
Group sizes Group SDs ANOVA (%) Welch (%) Kruskal-Wallis (%)
4/4/4 1/1/1 5.5 4.5 4.3
4/4/4 1/1/3 7.9 4.4 6.1
4/4/4 1/1/5 10.8 5.5 8.8
6/6/6 1/1/1 4.5 4.2 4.0
6/6/6 1/1/3 7.7 4.4 5.0
6/6/6 1/1/5 9.7 5.6 6.1
6/5/4 1/1/1 5.0 4.5 4.1
6/5/4 1/1/3 13.2 5.5 7.9
6/5/4 1/1/5 16.8 5.9 10.3
12/8/5 1/1/1 5.2 5.4 5.0
12/8/5 1/1/3 18.2 5.2 8.2
12/8/5 1/1/5 22.8 5.4 9.3
  • The Welch test stays close to 5% in every scenario, as it is designed to.
  • The ANOVA has too many false positives when the variances are unequal: up to 23% when the group with the largest variance is also the smallest. This is why rows with unequal variances should not be analyzed by an ANOVA, and it is what happens to the unequal-variance rows that are sorted into ne.
  • The Kruskal-Wallis test also has too many false positives when the variances are unequal (up to 10%), but fewer than the ANOVA. It assumes that the groups have the same shape and spread, so it is not a safe choice for rows with unequal variances either. This affects the unequal-variance rows that are sorted into nn.

The cost of a more robust test

When the assumptions of the ANOVA are met, it detects real differences more often than the Welch and Kruskal-Wallis tests. We simulated rows with equal variances in which the third group’s mean is 2 SD higher, and measured how often each test detects the difference (p < 0.05):

Power with equal variances (third group mean 2 SD higher)
Samples per group ANOVA (%) Welch (%) Kruskal-Wallis (%)
4 69.0 57.8 59.9
5 82.7 75.5 77.1
6 90.0 85.5 85.6
8 97.5 96.3 96.5

With 4 samples per group, the ANOVA detects the difference about 10 percentage points more often than the other two tests. The difference becomes small with 8 or more samples per group. This trade-off between power and robustness is the reason for choosing the test per row.

Other things to keep in mind

  • Interactions. Interaction p-values come from the ANOVA, so they are only available for rows sorted into ne. The Welch and Kruskal-Wallis tests are one-way tests on the combined groups (e.g. Female_KO, Female_WT, Male_KO, Male_WT).
  • Two kinds of p-value adjustment. The pairwise p-values (Tukey, Dunnett T3, Dunn) are adjusted for comparing several pairs of groups within one row. The padj columns additionally adjust for testing many rows (Benjamini-Hochberg), separately within each set.
  • Reproducibility of Dunnett T3. Its p-values are calculated with a random (Monte Carlo) method and can change very slightly between runs. Use set.seed() before the analysis to make them reproducible.
  • Wilcoxon p-values and R versions. From R 4.6.0, wilcox.test() calculates exact p-values for data with ties; earlier versions use an approximation. Wilcoxon p-values for data with ties (common in count data) therefore depend on the R version. Report the R version you used.
  • Rows with constant values. Rows where every value is the same can’t be tested and should be removed before the analysis.
  • Specialized tools. For RNA-seq count data, tools such as DESeq2, edgeR and limma model the properties of count data and share information between genes, which matters most with few samples. They also give interaction p-values for every gene. Statomatic is not a replacement for them.

Practical suggestions

  • Look at res$tests and the number of rows in each set. With few samples per group, keep in mind that the sorting is uncertain.
  • More samples per group make the sorting more reliable.
  • Report which tests were applied, the thresholds, the R version and the seed in your methods.

Reproducing the simulations

The simulations were run with statomatic 1.0.0 (R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24)). The script is installed with the package:

system.file("simulations", "sorting_simulations.R", package = "statomatic")
